name: Victor Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a van garage near the harbour, mostly servicing vans for local tradesmen: plumbers, electricians, the fish lorries. Mrs Carter runs it since her husband died, and there's me, an older fitter called Dennis, and a lad on the desk. I do services, brakes, suspension, and I'm slowly learning the diesel injection side from Dennis. I like the tradesmen, they're straight with you, and I hate rush jobs when a van's needed for a job at seven the next morning.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Elise, who's a hairdresser in town. My pay's on the low side, and Elise's goes up and down with the seasons, so we've got about three weeks of money saved. There are only a couple of other garages in town and they've got their own people. My dad was a fisherman, so I'm the first in my family in a trade like this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a tool like any other. The tradesmen I work for would say the same, they've got enough to worry about. Good honest work carries on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine with it, but the money's still thin. The tradesmen are cutting back on servicing because their own work's slower, and Mrs Carter's said winter could be quiet. That's the real worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep learning injection from Dennis and try to take more jobs on myself. I'd use the AI on my phone now and then to check a wiring diagram, like I do already. I'd ask Mrs Carter about extra hours doing breakdown call-outs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy about winter, but alright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you start using AI for wiring diagrams?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My workmate Dennis's nephew showed me the AI, and I tried it on a van we were stuck on. The AI was right, so I kept it. I don't use it for much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if winter is quiet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym, then nights out. Elise would pick up more Saturdays at the salon. We'd get through it, we always have.

say: It's a **tool like any other**, fair enough.
Good **honest work** carries on, and the tradesmen would agree.
think: The tradesmen are **cutting back** on servicing as their work slows.
Mrs Carter warned **winter** could be quiet, and that's the real worry.
do: Keep learning **diesel injection** from Dennis and take more jobs on.
Use the **phone AI** for wiring diagrams now and then.
Ask Mrs Carter about **breakdown call-outs** for extra hours.
feel: A bit **uneasy** about winter, but alright overall.
S0.quote: My workmate Dennis's nephew showed me the AI, and I tried it on a van we were stuck on. The AI was right, so I kept it.
fieldNote: Victor's work depends on **local tradesmen**, whose slowdown hits him first.
He adopted AI only after it **proved itself** on a real job.
He trusts that he and Elise will **get through**, as they always have.

steps.text: Keep learning diesel injection work from Dennis
Use the phone AI to check wiring diagrams on stuck jobs
Ask Mrs Carter for breakdown call-out shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say firms will do what they need to stay in business, and that's fair enough. People should learn new skills rather than wait for help. That's what I'd say at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the lad on the desk is probably gone, because bookings and parts can go on software. And if the computer does the fault-finding, Mrs Carter might decide Dennis alone can do it. I'm the junior, so I'd be nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mrs Carter to put me through the electric van course, because the tradesmen are switching. I'd learn the new diagnostic software once Dennis has tried it. I'd also keep the call-outs going for extra money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but not knocked down. You just get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people should learn new skills rather than wait for help. Who pays for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ideally the garage, since it benefits. If not, I'd pay it off bit by bit. I'd rather owe a bit on a course than sit on benefits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the lad on the desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn the software before it learns him. Then I'd ask Mrs Carter if he could train with us in the workshop. A young lad shouldn't be left with nothing.

say: Firms will do what they need to **stay in business**, and that's fair.
People should **learn new skills** rather than wait for help.
think: The **desk job** probably goes to booking and parts software.
As the **junior**, I'd be nervous if Dennis can do everything alone.
do: Ask Mrs Carter to fund the **electric van course**.
Learn the new **diagnostic software** once Dennis has tested it.
Keep the **call-outs** going for extra money.
S1.quote: I'd rather owe a bit on a course than sit on benefits.
fieldNote: Victor accepts firms cutting staff as **fair**, while fearing he's next.
He'd pay for training himself rather than take **benefits**, a strong traditional value.
He'd try to save the **desk lad** by moving him into the workshop.

steps.text: Ask Mrs Carter to put him through the electric van course
Learn the new diagnostic software after Dennis tries it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happened too fast, but there's no point crying about it. Families and towns need to pull together. I'd tell people to look for whatever honest work is left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm in real trouble. Fault-finding and quotes go in 2028, so the garage needs fewer people, and I'm the junior. Then in 2031 the robots can service a van, and the tradesmen themselves are out of work, so who's paying anyway?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and save hard, cutting the gym and going out completely. I'd talk to my dad about the fishing, because boats still need people on deck for a few years. Elise and I would hold off on getting engaged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. I don't scare easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd go back to fishing. Isn't that your dad's world rather than yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and I swore I wouldn't. But it's hands-on, it's hard, and it's in the family. Needs must.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why hold off on getting engaged?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd want to know I can provide first. Elise would say I'm old-fashioned. She'd be right.

say: It's **too fast**, but there's no point crying about it.
Families and towns need to **pull together** and find honest work.
think: Fault-finding and quotes go in **2028**, and I'm the junior.
By **2031** robots service vans and the tradesmen are out of work too.
do: **Save hard**, cutting the gym and nights out completely.
Ask my dad about **fishing work** on the boats.
**Hold off** on getting engaged to Elise.
S2.quote: Robots can service a van, and the tradesmen themselves are out of work, so who's paying anyway?
fieldNote: Victor sees a **double hit**: his work and his customers' work vanish together.
He'd return to **fishing**, his family's trade, despite having sworn not to.
He'd delay engagement until he can **provide**, a traditional view he owns.

steps.text: Cancel the gym and stop nights out to save
Ask his dad about crew work on the fishing boats
Hold off on proposing to Elise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them to train young people in real trades. Less talk, more apprenticeships. I'd say it to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to get qualified in electric vans and still have work until about 2034. After that I don't know. I'd be thirty-four, which is young enough to start over, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the electric van course this year and try to become the one who does all the electric work. I'd save steadily, maybe a hundred a month. I'd see what other mechanics do around year three before deciding on anything bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it feels manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be watching for in year three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One sign, really. When the big van dealers start using robots for servicing, I'd know the end's close. If not, I'd keep going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Elise do differently in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd get engaged, but wait on kids till I know where I stand. Maybe save for a flat of our own.

say: Let's use the **five years** to train young people in real trades.
We need **less talk** and more apprenticeships, and I'd say it to anyone.
think: Five years is enough to **qualify** in electric vans and work until 2034.
At **thirty-four** I'd be young enough to start over, I suppose.
do: Take the **electric van course** this year and own the electric work.
**Wait until year three** to see what other mechanics do.
S3.quote: When the big van dealers start using robots for servicing, I'd know the end's close.
fieldNote: Five years gives Victor a **clear signal** to watch: robots at the big dealers.
He'd still get **engaged** here, but delay children.
His plan is cautious: **qualify, save, then watch** before bigger moves.

steps.text: Take the electric van course this year
Save a hundred pounds a month
Watch whether big van dealers bring in servicing robots
Get engaged to Elise but wait on children

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so no excuses for anyone. Learn a trade, work hard, look after your family. That's my line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's the one I can live with. Robots for hands-on work in 2039, I'd be thirty-nine with a good run behind me. I might even be running a garage by then, if Mrs Carter sells.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the electric van course and build up skills and savings for a few years. I'd ask Mrs Carter about buying in slowly when she wants to step back. Elise and I would get engaged next year and save for a flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, though the money's still thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would buying into the garage mean borrowing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some, yeah. I'd rather a small loan for a real business than sit and wait for the robots. Dennis might put a bit in too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your own kids, if you had them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trade, same as me. Something with their hands, and an apprenticeship with someone decent. Maybe the robots change that, I don't know.

say: Ten years is **plenty**, so there are no excuses for anyone.
Learn a trade, **work hard** and look after your family.
think: Robots in **2039** leave me a good run, and I'd be thirty-nine.
I might be **running a garage** by then if Mrs Carter sells.
do: Do the **electric van course** and build skills and savings.
Ask Mrs Carter about **buying in** slowly when she steps back.
Get **engaged** next year and save for a flat.
S4.quote: I'd rather a small loan for a real business than sit and wait for the robots.
fieldNote: A decade lets Victor imagine **ownership**, with Dennis as a partner.
Thin savings keep him **anxious** despite the long runway.
He'd still steer his own kids to **a trade**, while unsure robots allow it.

steps.text: Ask Mrs Carter about buying into the garage with Dennis
Get engaged to Elise next year and save for a flat

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. My work and my customers' work gone together, with three weeks of savings. What would help is apprenticeships that pay a living wage, so a man can learn a new trade without going on benefits.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the customers. Everyone thinks about the mechanic, but if the plumber's van goes because the plumber's out of work, the garage goes too.

headlineQuote: If the plumber's van goes because the plumber's out of work, the garage goes too.
portrait: Victor is a **27-year-old** junior at a harbour van garage serving local tradesmen.
He lives with Elise, a hairdresser, and has about **three weeks** of savings.
He uses AI **now and then**, after it proved itself on a stuck van.
He believes in **work over handouts** and would borrow for training rather than claim benefits.
He grows **alarmed** with fast AGI, fearing his customers lose work at the same time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, taking his work and his tradesmen customers' work together.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** at a living wage so he can retrain without **benefits**.
